catalog_citation: Chirikba, Viacheslav A. (2003). Abkhaz. Languages of the World/Materials 119. Muenchen: LINCOM Europa.
catalog_locator: section 1.4 'Stress', pp. 21-22 (archive.org item chirikbaabkhaz, PDF page 12-13)
catalog_quote: 1.4. Stress. Abkhaz is characterized by strong dynamic stress, which can fall on any syllable in polysyllabic words. Longer words can have a secondary stress. Less usually, two syllables in a long word can be equally stressed. Stress distinguishes many otherwise homophonic words and word-forms, cf. áč'a 'quail' – a-č'á 'wheat; bread'; á-la 'eye' – a-lá 'dog'; áħºa 'sword' – a-ħºá 'pig, swine'; á-pa-ra 'to jump' – a-pára 'money' – a-pa-rá 'to knit'. According to Dybo (1989) and Spruit (1986: 37-79), every syllable (including monoconsonantal morphemes) in Abkhaz can be assigned a certain prosodic valence (high or low, or in other terminology, dominant or recessive). It is the combinations of syllables each possessing its own valence, which determine the stress pattern of the given word(-form). According to Dybo, this accentual model could be a transformation of an older tonal system.

sources.citation: Andersson, Samuel (2024). The phonetics and phonology of Abkhaz word stress. PhD dissertation, Yale University. (lingbuzz 008484)
sources.quote: p.4: 'There are no window restrictions ... where stress must be close to a word edge, no sonority restrictions on stress assignment, and there is no weight sensitivity ... The placement of surface stress depends only on the prosodic properties of the constituent morphemes in a word, as determined by Dybo's Rule (Dybo 1977)'. p.92: 'Abkhaz has contrastive stress, meaning that there are segmentally identical words which are distinguished only by contrasts in where primary stress falls' ([á-la] 'eye' vs [a-lá] 'dog'). p.99: 'In actual Abkhaz, however, we find no such weight restrictions. sources.citation: Wolfe, Andrew M. (2000). Iterativity in Abkhaz stress. Ms., Harvard University. (lingbuzz 007175)
sources.quote: 'Abkhaz's lexical stress system uses an algorithm first stated by Dybo 1977 which gives word stress to the leftmost accented syllable not followed by another accented syllable ... accent is a memorized quality of individual morphemes.' (1) Dybo's Rule (from Spruit): '... If there is no accent in the word, stress falls on the last syllable of the word.'
